nameStory: Marsh Thyme-moss gets its name from its oval-shaped leaves that resemble tiny thyme herb leaves, and its preference for wet, marshy habitats. The scientific name 'ellipticum' refers to these distinctive elliptical leaf shapes that help distinguish it from its moss cousins.
description: Marsh Thyme-moss is a delicate, bright green moss that forms loose patches or scattered colonies in wet areas. It grows in small tufts reaching about 1-2 inches tall, with distinctly oval leaves arranged in a somewhat flattened pattern along its stems. When moist, this moss has a fresh, vibrant green color that can fade to yellowish-green when dry.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to elliptical leaves that are broader than most mosses, with a distinctly rounded tip and visible midrib running down the center - they feel slightly papery when dry

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, scattered patches rather than dense cushions, with individual stems standing somewhat upright but not tightly packed together

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in consistently moist to wet areas - if the ground isn't damp underfoot, you're probably looking at a different moss

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright emerald green when wet, shifting to a duller yellow-green when dry, with leaves that appear almost translucent at the edges

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and springy when moist, becoming slightly crispy and brittle to the touch when dried out

habitat: Look for Marsh Thyme-moss in consistently wet areas like stream banks, seepage areas, wet meadows, and the soggy edges of ponds or marshes throughout New England. It prefers mineral-rich soils and is often found where groundwater seeps to the surface. This moss thrives in areas that stay moist even during dry spells.

seasonality.spring: Most visible and vibrant as snowmelt provides abundant moisture, showing its brightest green coloration. New growth appears fresh and the leaves look plump and healthy.
seasonality.summer: May appear less vibrant during dry periods, taking on yellowish tones, but remains green in consistently wet spots. Sporophytes (spore capsules) may be present on thin stalks.
seasonality.fall: Often experiences a second flush of bright color as autumn rains return, making it easier to spot again. The contrast with dying surrounding vegetation makes it stand out.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow in milder periods, though growth slows significantly. The moss can survive freezing but appears dormant and less colorful.

funFact: Despite being called 'Marsh' Thyme-moss, it's incredibly rare in New England with only one recorded observation - making it potentially rarer to spot than some orchids or other 'exotic' plants that nature lovers actively seek out!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other thyme-mosses in wet areas, but Marsh Thyme-moss has distinctly broader, more oval leaves compared to the narrower, more pointed leaves of Woodsy Thyme-moss. Remember: 'Marsh' means broader, rounder leaves in marshy spots.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this moss in New England (only one recorded observation) suggests it may be at the edge of its natural range here, or that it's easily overlooked by botanists. Finding it would be a significant botanical discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives, Marsh Thyme-moss has the broadest, most elliptical leaves - Woodsy Thyme-moss has more pointed leaves, while Wavy-leaf Moss has distinctly wavy leaf edges. The oval leaf shape is really the key feature that sets Marsh Thyme-moss apart from its cousins in the Plagiomnium family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its thyme-moss relatives, Woodsy Thyme-moss has the most orderly, shingle-like leaf arrangement compared to Wavy-leaf Moss's more irregular, wavy-edged leaves.

Wavy-leaf Moss stands out from its thyme-moss relatives primarily by those distinctive wavy, toothed leaf margins - Woodsy Thyme-moss has smoother leaf edges, while Marsh Thyme-moss prefers wetter areas and has more pointed leaves.
Unlike its relatives Woodsy Thyme-moss (found in forests) and Marsh Thyme-moss (found in wetlands), Alpine thyme-moss is strictly a high-elevation specialist.
